messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Triggers

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Carlos is a seventy-year-old welder, a widower, who came to the United States from El Salvador forty years ago. He sought help at the insistence of his daughter, who had grown alarmed by his increasing isolation and the way he would sometimes freeze, mid-weld, his hands trembling as if he had heard something no one else could hear. The event that haunts him happened in his early twenties, during the Salvadoran Civil War. He was detained by a paramilitary squad and held for three days in a small, windowless room. They beat him, burned his forearms with the tips of their cigarettes, and at one point held a pistol to his temple and pulled the trigger on an empty chamber. They did this twice. The third time, the gun fired, but the bullet passed through the fleshy part of his shoulder rather than his skull. He survived because he had been compliant, had answered their questions, had not fought back. That is what he tells himself. He was compliant, and that is why he lives. But he also tells himself something else: that he should have done more, that he should have tried to escape or fight, that his survival was a kind of cowardice.

The memory of that room does not feel like a memory. When it comes, it comes as a complete sensory immersion: the smell of sweat and diesel, the pressure of the wall against his back, the cold metal of the gun barrel against his temple. He cannot describe it to his daughter without losing the thread, his sentences breaking apart, his hands beginning to shake as if the event were still happening. And when the memory is present, it is not the fear that overwhelms him first—it is the rage. A hot, wordless fury at the men, at himself, at the world that let it happen. He feels it in his chest, a pressure that demands release, but he has nowhere to put it. So he pushes the memory away. He tries hard not to think about it. He tells himself it is over, it is in the past, but the memory does not listen.

The triggers are everywhere, though he did not always recognize them. A sudden loud noise—a car backfiring, a dropped metal beam in the workshop—will send him back into that room. But the most insidious trigger is the feeling of entrapment, of having no options. It happens when he is stuck in traffic, when a door closes behind him in a small bathroom, when his boss gives him an order he cannot refuse. In those moments, the present dissolves and he is twenty-three again, helpless. And each time that happens, his old belief hardens further: you can never know who will harm you. He has come to see threat in ordinary faces, in the casual authority of a foreman, in the raised voice of a stranger. The world, he is certain, is full of people waiting for him to be weak.

When he feels threatened, his body remembers the solution that saved him once: compliance. He becomes overly agreeable, his voice softening, his shoulders rounding, his answers becoming what he thinks the other person wants to hear. He does this automatically, even with his daughter, even with his doctor. He hates himself for it. He thinks, I will never forgive myself for not doing more to stop what happened, and then he thinks, The event happened because of the way I acted. These appraisals loop together, feeding each other, and they drive him back into the same compliant posture. The more he blames himself, the more he expects danger, and the more he expects danger, the more he scans for it. A raised voice in the grocery store. A man walking too close behind him. Each perceived threat triggers the memory, and the memory triggers the rage, and the rage triggers the urge to suppress, and the suppression leaves him exhausted and hollow.

Over the months, his world has narrowed. He no longer goes to the hardware store on weekends. He avoids the freeway during rush hour. At work, he has started taking longer breaks in the supply closet—a small, windowless space that should feel like a trap but somehow feels safer because he chose it. His daughter has noticed that he flinches when she knocks on his door. He does not tell her about the nights when he lies awake, the gunshot sound echoing in his ears, the rage building until he has to get up and walk around the block. He does not tell her that sometimes, in the middle of a weld, he feels the heat on his forearms and has to stop because his hands are shaking too much to hold the torch steady.

What finally brought him to the clinic was a moment at work last month. His foreman, a heavyset man with a loud voice, asked him to redo a weld. Carlos said yes. He said yes too quickly, too softly, and the foreman looked at him strangely. Later that day, Carlos found himself in the supply closet, his back against the wall, his heart pounding, the memory so vivid he could smell the diesel. He stayed there for twenty minutes. When he came out, his supervisor asked if he was okay, and Carlos said yes again, the same compliant yes, and he hated himself so much that he called his daughter that night. He is afraid of what he might do if the rage ever breaks through. He is afraid that one day he will not be able to push the memory away. He is hoping, though he cannot quite say it, that someone will tell him it was not his fault.
